description_full: AngloGold Ashanti plc operates as a gold mining company in Africa, Australia, and the Americas. It explores for gold, as well as by-products, including silver and sulphuric acid. The company's flagship property includes 100% owned the Geita mine located in the Lake Victoria goldfields of the Geita region in northwestern Tanzania. AngloGold Ashanti plc was incorporated in 1944 and is headquartered in Greenwood Village, Colorado.

Each employee generates $88K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 16× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: AngloGold Ashanti PLC is a large-cap basic materials business with a $43.7B market cap on $9.9B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +47% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +20.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $3.3B in free cash flow — roughly 34 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.51× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 38× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 44% operating margin runs 35pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.41x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 2.0% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 60% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.54 vs 5y 0.80), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $215.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2020 crash, 52% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 19% below its DCF fair value of $106, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $80.24 to $143 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 11.2 vs 16.3, EV/EBITDA 6.1 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 13.1 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $114 on average, 32% above the price.
The price implies 6.1% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.00).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 34% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.51x.
ROE of 39% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $880.0M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 46.9% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 9.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
It has missed earnings estimates by 2.4% on average.
Analysts expect 13.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 74%.
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (5.2% in dividends).
people: With about 38,000 employees, each generates about $260K of revenue, 0.4x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 46.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $88K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.1M (16x revenue per employee).
